1	# Prose and durable text
2	
3	How long-lived text is written on this project: the prose shape, the punctuation rules, and the
4	commit-title identity. Read this before writing durable text (notes files, commit messages, doc
5	comments, the cycle-record).
6	
7	Universal file, shared with the template repository. A proposed change is edited here and converges
8	at the template ([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)). Project-local
9	content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).
10	
11	## Prose form
12	
13	([why](rationale.md#prose-form))
14	
15	Long-lived prose on this project follows one basic shape: a short intro that explains the *why* or
16	the high-level *what*, sharpened to a *problem statement* where a surface calls for one (see
17	[Problem-first shape](#problem-first-shape)), then a `-` bullet list for the details. The width
18	numbers and the wrap discipline live in [Line widths](#line-widths) below, their one home. One fact
19	per bullet or sub-bullet beats a paragraph packing several. Avoid wall-of-prose paragraphs: they
20	hide the structure that bullets make scannable. Punctuation that joins clauses without naming their
21	relationship is the same failure at sentence scale. See [Semicolons](#semicolons) and [Typeable
22	punctuation only](#typeable-punctuation-only).
23	
24	Surfaces that use this shape:
25	
26	- Module / function / struct / field doc comments in `.rs` files. See [Doc
27	  comments](code.md#doc-comments-on-every-file-function-and-method).
28	- Commit message bodies (both work-repo and agent-repo). The title is the commit-specific add-on.
29	  See [The per-rung flow](../AGENTS.md#the-per-rung-flow).
30	- The cycle-record, `TODO.md > ## In Progress`. See [The In Progress
31	  block](notes.md#the-in-progress-block).
32	- Todo entries in `TODO.md` when an entry needs more than one line of detail. Pure one-liners are
33	  still fine.
34	
35	Bullet *content* differs by surface:
36	
37	- **Commit bodies**: the [Problem-first shape](#problem-first-shape) for finished work, arranged by
38	  [Commit-body form](#commit-body-form) below. What is specific to a commit:
39	  - the problem statement defines any word the title assumes, since the title is what a reader meets
40	    first and it answers the problem
41	  - **no file list.** The diff and `git show --stat` are the mechanical record, so restating them is
42	    a second copy that can drift from the first. An import of a thousand files is one change
43	  - these are claims a reader has to follow, so they are sentences rather than fragments. A bullet
44	    wanting a paragraph belongs in the cycle-record instead
45	  - the **deliberation** stays out: alternatives weighed, evidence, dates, costs accepted. Those
46	    live in the cycle-record, the `## Todo` entry, and the session the `ochid:` trailer names, each
47	    reachable from the commit by construction. The problem itself is a *why* and belongs here
48	- **Cycle-record / todo**: bullets are conceptual (design points, structural notes, the "what landed
49	  and why" at a notch above file-list granularity). Never a copy of the commit's edit list. The diff
50	  is the mechanical record, the commit body the problem and solution, the cycle-record the design
51	  thinking, and none restates another.
52	- **Doc comments**: bullets are whatever structure fits (fields, cases, invariants).
53	
54	### Leads are labels, unmarked
55	
56	In a list item or a numbered step, a lead is a short label ending in a colon, with no markup, and
57	the sentence after it is complete without it:
58	
59	```
60	1. Backfill: fill every as-built ladder whose commits have landed, before anything else.
61	```
62	
63	- Label names, sentence instructs: a reader's eye takes bold at the head of an item as the item's
64	  name and resumes at the plain text expecting a full sentence, so a bold lead that is the
65	  sentence's own verb or subject (`**Backfill** every as-built ladder ...`) loses its imperative to
66	  the reader who skips it. Measured 2026-08-21, at the review of the rule that example is from: the
67	  reviewer read "every as-built ladder" and stopped, with nothing telling them what to do.
68	- The inverted case: a rule stated in bold is the same failure inverted. When the bold is a whole
69	  sentence and the plain text is commentary, the reader who skips bold reads the commentary as the
70	  rule. The fix is the same: a short name as the label, the rule as the plain sentence. The hard
71	  rules in AGENTS.md are the instance, and the names they gained are greppable and survive a
72	  renumbering.
73	- Definitions: the same shape, `Term: what it means.` A period after a bold term (`**Term.** ...`)
74	  reads as a heading, which is the label reading again.
75	- No markup on the label: bold is what makes the eye treat the lead as a heading and skip it, and
76	  the agent-files are read by an agent, which needs no emphasis. The colon alone marks the label
77	  (wink, 2026-08-21).
78	- The price: one word of redundancy, paid on purpose: the label is skippable, the sentence is not.
79	
80	### One spelling per term
81	
82	A defined term has one spelling, everywhere: `work-repo` and `agent-repo` are always hyphenated,
83	`agent-files`, `version-of-record`, `dual-repo`, and `as-built` likewise, and no rule varies the
84	spelling by how the term is used. Terminology in AGENTS.md defines the terms, and this section is
85	where the spelling rule lives, since a glossary is read for meaning rather than for spelling.
86	
87	### Bullet form
88	
89	A bullet is a full sentence, capitalized and ending in a period or question mark, unless the list
90	is a plain list of things (files, names, options), which takes neither. A list is all one or all
91	the other. A sentence never opens with a lower-case name (`squash-push`, `rationale.md`), it is
92	recast so the name is not the first word.
93	
94	### Line widths
95	
96	Every width number lives here and nowhere else: the other files and sections link here rather than
97	restating one, so a change is a single edit and the copies cannot drift. Consolidated 2026-08-09,
98	when the body width moved and the restatements had to be hunted.
99	
100	- **Prose**, all durable text: wrap at <=100 cols, bullet continuations indented two spaces.
101	- **Source**, doc comments and inline comments included: <=100 cols, which is rustfmt's default
102	  `max_width` (enforcement notes in [code.md](code.md#line-width)).
103	- **Commit titles**: <=50 chars.
104	- **Commit bodies**: <=75 cols, the Linux kernel patch standard. It replaced git's older 72
105	  convention here 2026-08-09, and published bodies keep the wrap they shipped with.
106	
107	The widths are wrap defaults, not absolutes (the title cap excepted). Existing text re-wraps when
108	touched, no mass sweeps. Write to the full width: wrap near the limit rather than imitating the
109	narrow wrap of older text, and a line that reads better long stays long (an URL, a literal report
110	row, indented code in a comment).
111	
112	### Problem-first shape
113	
114	`## In Progress` cycle blocks, `## Todo` entries, and commit bodies use a sharper form of the same
115	shape: a problem, then how it is answered, then the steps that get there.
116	
117	- **Problem statement** (the why): one or two sentences. Don't pad with intent, don't restate what
118	  follows it.
119	- **Solution statement** (the what/how): what is done about the problem, in broad terms, answering
120	  whatever question the problem statement raises. Surface-specific rules are in [Bullet content
121	  differs by surface](#prose-form) above.
122	- **Plan bullets** (the what/when), the steps. Formality differs by surface:
123	  - In Progress: a committed ladder, one step per commit. See [Conventional-commit
124	    shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--commit) for the per-step title + `(current)` /
125	    `(done)` form.
126	  - Todo entries: rough informal bullets, no numbering, formalized only when the entry is picked up
127	    into a cycle.
128	
129	**Timing decides whether the solution statement is provisional, not whether it is written.** A cycle
130	writes one at Preparation, before the work, and revises it as steps land. The close-out's commit
131	body carries the final one. A `## Todo` entry's is provisional in the same way. Only a commit body's
132	is settled, because a commit is finished by the time it has one. The earlier rule here said a plan
133	was for work not yet done and a solution for work that is, which left a cycle unable to say at its
134	opening what it intended to do.
135	
136	### Commit-body form
137	
138	The specimen is [commit-model.md](commit-model.md). A commit body is the [Problem-first
139	shape](#problem-first-shape) with one addition: a body whose
140	problem has several sub-problems arranges them by a fixed recursion, so a reader knows what any
141	bullet is from its marker and its depth. The earlier statement, "a problem statement then a solution
142	statement, both broad", left that arrangement to taste, and taste converged slowly and separately.
143	
144	- **An intro paragraph states the general problem**, and defines any word the title assumes. It is
145	  mandatory. [Prose form](#prose-form) wants it regardless, and a body opening on a bullet is a body
146	  a `--body` flag can mistake for an option. The problem is *this commit's*, never the cycle's: the
147	  cycle's problem lives in the In Progress block, and a body whose problems outnumber what the diff
148	  resolves is describing something larger than the commit.
149	- **`*` bullets are the problem's facets**: sub-problems that decompose the intro's general problem,
150	  not a grab-bag of unrelated fixes. A body reaching for unrelated problem bullets is usually asking
151	  to be more than one commit.
152	- **`-` bullets are solutions**, and every `-` sits under a `*`, solving that facet. A `-` with no
153	  `*` above it reads as a solution to nothing, so there are no top-level solutions: a solution that
154	  retires every facet at once is written under each, or the facets are one.
155	- **One facet is the trivial commit**: the intro, one `*`, one or more `-` under it. Not a second
156	  form, the general form at its smallest.
157	- **A bookend body is a pointer**: an opening or closing commit resolves no problem of its own, so
158	  its body is the intro paragraph alone, naming the cycle by its title and pointing at its record,
159	  the In Progress block. No `*`, no `-`.
160	
161	**The markers are typed on purpose**: `*` always means problem, `-` always means solution, and the
162	pairing is what a reader counts on: the `-` answers the `*` above it, with no rule to consult. The
163	typing also keeps history greppable (`^\* ` finds every facet, `^ - ` every solution). Bodies are
164	read as plain text, in `jj log` and in terminals, where the markers survive, and if a renderer ever
165	flattens them the indentation still carries the structure. So the mixed markers are deliberate, and
166	a linter's consistent-marker rule is wrong to normalize them.
167	
168	Unchanged by this: no version in title or body, no file list, no deliberation, titles per
169	[Conventional-commit shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--commit).
170	
171	### Semicolons
172	
173	Prose carries no semicolons. A semicolon appears only in code (code spans, fenced code, source
174	files), where it is syntax rather than prose. The structure a semicolon would have joined is written
175	explicitly instead:
176	
177	- **Two claims** take a period, each half standing as its own sentence ("The diff empties. The
178	  history keeps the record.").
179	- **A continuation** takes a comma with a conjunction, when one half carries the other's thought
180	  onward rather than making its own claim.
181	- **A list hiding in prose** (`A; B; C` inside a sentence or bullet) breaks into sub-bullets so the
182	  structure shows. List items that themselves contain commas restructure the same way rather than
183	  separating with semicolons.
184	
185	The code allowance is why a bare byte scan cannot enforce the rule: a checker blanks the code first,
186	then expects zero.
187	
188	The agent-files (`AGENTS.md`, `custom*`, `agent-data/*`) carry no historical exemption and are swept
189	to zero. Any other historical file keeps its existing semicolons only until it is touched: a commit
190	that edits a file makes that whole file's prose semicolons owed, code spans exempt, and the cycle
191	pays them in a penultimate rung of its own, or in its one commit when single-step, using the joins
192	above, so the touching rung's diff reads as its change alone. What is owed still follows from
193	touching the file, and only the payment moves. New prose is written correct and is never a sweep
194	item. A file whose count means rewriting rather than repunctuating becomes its own cycle. Files
195	outside a cycle's diff are never converted, since that is a sweep and sweeps are their own cycle.
196	Source-file comments are prose under this rule (see [code.md](code.md#comments-are-prose)).
197	
198	### Typeable punctuation only
199	
200	Durable text uses punctuation that can be typed at a terminal. The prohibition is on *authoring*,
201	not presence: a file may legitimately hold a banned character it transcribed (see below), so a byte
202	scan is not the rule and a sweep needs the authored/transcribed judgment. Banned from authoring:
203	`—`, `–`, `…`, `→`. None can be entered without a compose key or a paste, so none can be grepped
204	for, and an em dash next to option syntax reads as another flag. Like the semicolon rule above, the
205	agent-files are swept to zero and any other file converts whole when a cycle touches it, paid in
206	the same penultimate rung as the semicolons (specimens and transcriptions aside, below). A banned
207	character costs nothing to write and is paid on every read, so the rule is not softer than that.
208	
209	`…` becomes `...` and `→` becomes `->`. The dashes have no single replacement, because an em dash
210	usually stands in for a structural decision that was not made. Make the decision:
211	
212	- **A bullet's title and its body sharing a line** is a heading and a paragraph. Make the body
213	  sub-bullets.
214	- **A term and its definition** (`jj diff`, `<base>`, a flag) takes a colon, which keeps a glossary
215	  or a command list at one line per entry.
216	- **A prose aside** takes a comma, parentheses, or two sentences. Often the aside should just go.
217	
218	Converting a heading moves its anchor. The em dash strips but the spaces on both sides survive, so
219	`## A — B` slugs to `#a--b` while its colon form slugs to `#a-b` (see [Markdown anchor
220	links](notes.md#markdown-anchor-links)). Re-point inbound links in the same commit.
221	
222	Scope is the same as [Speculation marker](#speculation-marker), plus commit titles and everything
223	under `src/`: doc comments, inline comments, and any user-visible string. Source is the surface a
224	human edits and greps most, so an untypeable character costs more there than in prose. A code span
225	is not exempt by itself. Naming the character is a specimen and stays, which is how this section
226	names them. A banned character doing a job is a use and converts: `` `.expect(…)` `` becomes
227	`` `.expect(...)` ``.
228	
229	Text quoted from outside this repo's prose (tool output, an error message, an already-published
230	commit title) is transcribed, not written, so it keeps its characters, whether or not it sits in a
231	code span. It matters most for commit titles: converting one stops it matching `git log --grep` and
232	breaks the verbatim identity that [Conventional-commit
233	shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--commit) requires between a commit title and its ladder
234	rung.
235	
236	### Conventional-commit shape (ladder / commit)
237	
238	([why](rationale.md#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--commit))
239	
240	A ladder step and its commit description share a *title* shape, a [Conventional
241	Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/) title (`<type>: <desc>`, an optional
242	`(scope)` after the type: `feat(push): ...`) over [Prose form](#prose-form) detail. They differ in
243	the title's marker (below) and in bullet *content*: commit bodies take the [Commit-body
244	form](#commit-body-form), the ladder's are conceptual (see "Bullet *content* differs by surface"
245	above). The shared template:
246	
247	```
248	<title>                          # <title> is the commit's `<type>: <desc>`
249	<optional prose intro>
250	  - <optional item>
251	    <optional prose intro>
252	      - <optional sub-item>
253	      ...
254	```
255	
256	The two surfaces apply it as:
257	
258	- **Ladder step** (`TODO.md` `## In Progress`): the rung is `- [<title>][M] (marker)`: the title
259	  reference-linked to the rung's subsection via `[M]: #<slug>` in the file's `# References` (the
260	  closing rung linked like the rest), and the `(current)` / `(done)` marker. Its position in the
261	  list is its position in the ladder. The last rung is the close-out and its text says so. Detail
262	  lives not on the rung but in the block's `Ladder details` subsection headed by the rung's exact
263	  title (see the protocol's [Opening](../AGENTS.md#opening)), bulleted, never `;`-joined inline.
264	- **Commit description**: no prefix. The title is the first line, and the body is the prose (see
265	  [Commit description](../AGENTS.md#commit-description)).
266	
267	The title is **identical** across both for a given step, so a step's ladder entry and its commit
268	title line up verbatim. A `Ladder details` subsection heading carries the same title, a third
269	surface on every rung (the closing rung's exists only when close-out gotchas occurred: see the
270	protocol's [Opening](../AGENTS.md#opening)). Pick the commit title first and reuse it.
271	
272	That identity is **per step**, not per cycle: each step in a cycle gets its own distinct descriptive
273	title, never one shared cycle title uniquified by a step marker. The block's title heading carries
274	the *cycle title*, the bare name no multi-step commit carries (see the bookends below). To keep a
275	cycle's commits collectable with one `git log --grep`, give the step titles a common greppable stem
276	(e.g. `config loader`).
277	
278	**Cycle bookend titles**: a multi-step cycle's bookend commits are the cycle title plus a suffix, "
279	opening" and " closing", same type (`feat: dynamic warmup opening` /
280	`feat: dynamic warmup closing`), so one `git log --grep "<cycle title>"` returns the pair that
281	brackets the ladder. The bare cycle title is the cycle's *name*: the block's title heading carries
282	it, and no multi-step commit does, which is also what keeps the closing rung's subsection anchor
283	clear of the title heading's. A single-step cycle's one commit is the cycle and keeps the bare
284	title, in both repos and in its one ladder rung ([Cycle shape](../AGENTS.md#cycle-shape)). The type
285	repeats across the pair even though the bookends are mostly bookkeeping: identical prefixes make
286	them scannable. Rungs between keep their own titles on the stem.
287	
288	### Commit titles and descriptions
289	
290	([why](rationale.md#commit-titles-and-descriptions))
291	
292	The vocabulary over the structure: [Conventional-commit
293	shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--commit) holds what a title and body are shaped like, and
294	this section holds what may fill them. The title is a [Conventional
295	Commit](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/), `<type>: <short description>` with an optional
296	`(scope)`, at the width in [Line widths](#line-widths). The body is the [Commit-body
297	form](#commit-body-form), wrapped per Line widths, with no version in title or body, no file list,
298	and no deliberation. `vc-x1 push` gives both repos' commits the same title and body. `ochid:` is
299	the body's last line, stamped by push, and a breaking change uses the hyphenated
300	`BREAKING-CHANGE:` trailer key.
301	
302	#### Conventional commit types
303	
304	The common types: `feat`, `fix`, `refactor`, `test`, `docs`, `chore`. A type beyond the common set
305	is a declared one ([Project-declared types](#project-declared-types)), and a title check admits
306	exactly the two vocabularies.
307	
308	#### Conventional commit scopes
309	
310	A scope names a component as its user would name it (a subcommand, a repo), never a file or
311	directory, and is omitted when there is none. A declared type's scope slot carries its
312	declaration's vocabulary instead ([Project-declared types](#project-declared-types)).
313	
314	#### Project-declared types
315	
316	Beyond the common types, a project may declare its own when a recurring kind of work deserves one
317	searchable token. The declaration names the type, its scope vocabulary, and its description
318	grammar, so a reader can parse the titles and a title check can admit them by name, and the scope
319	slot then carries what the declaration says rather than a component. A project's own declarations
320	live in its `custom.md`, and the set declares for itself:
321	
322	- `agent-files`, the set's own lifecycle: `agent-files(<scope>): vX.Y.Z`, the description being the
323	  agent-files version in its `v` spelling ([Agent-files
324	  version](versioning.md#agent-files-version)), which keeps the formulaic titles unique and is the
325	  one version a title may carry ([Versions live in the version-of-record
326	  only](#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only)).
327	  - The two scopes:
328	    - `proposal`, outbound work for others to adopt. The cycle bumps the agent-files version, and
329	      the title names the new one.
330	    - `adoption`, inbound. The cycle copies the source's version file, and the title names what it
331	      took.
332	  - Who proposed to whom, or adopted from whom, is the message record's `from:` and `to:`, never
333	    the title's.
334	  - `git log --grep 'agent-files('` finds every agent-files title, the recurring type being the
335	    token that collects the thread.
336	
337	### Steps are named, not numbered
338	
339	A step has a title and no number. Nothing in a ladder rung or a commit gives a step an ordinal: a
340	rung's place in the list already *is* its place in the ladder, so a number beside it would restate
341	the position and then have to be maintained.
342	
343	- **The title is the identifier.** A record points at a step by its title, a plain greppable
344	  mention, which is why the title is verbatim-identical across the three surfaces.
345	- **Unambiguous, not globally unique.** Two titles must be distinguishable where a title is
346	  resolved: within its own cycle's block, so a ladder rung names one step and its subsection heading
347	  one anchor, since a repeated slug silently dedupes to the first one. Across the repo's history a
348	  title may repeat.
349	- **Nothing renumbers.** Inserting, reordering or dropping a step edits the ladder list and nothing
350	  else. On an unlanded topic bookmark the rungs that already committed an older ladder come along.
351	  See [Cycles run on a bookmark](../AGENTS.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark).
352	- **`## Todo` is ordered, not numbered**: priority is file order ([Todo
353	  format](notes.md#todo-format)), so no rank number exists to be cited (the numbered form retired
354	  2026-08-27).
355	
356	### Versions live in the version-of-record only
357	
358	No version appears in durable prose: not in a ladder rung, a commit title, or a commit body. The
359	manifest is the version's only written home (see [versioning.md](versioning.md)), and a commit's
360	version is read from that file at that commit
361	([why](rationale.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only)). The one exception is the set's
362	own version in an `agent-files` title, wherever that title appears ([Project-declared
363	types](#project-declared-types)): it names an agreed text, not a build, and naming which is the
364	title's job.
365	
366	**No surface records a version.** Which commit a version names is read from the manifest at that
367	commit, and "what shipped in 0.42.0" is answered by `git log` on the manifest, not by a list kept in
368	prose. The earlier chores as-built rungs and `## Done` entries carried versions beside commit SHAs,
369	and retired with the records they lived in ([Cycle-record](../AGENTS.md#cycle-record)).
370	
371	## Agent-files name no project
372	
373	An agent-file states rules and mechanisms. It never names an adopter, an adopter's history, or an
374	adopter's versions. The vc-x1 *CLI* and its versions are tool facts every adopter shares and stay.
375	What is barred is an adopter's repo appearing in universal text
376	([why](rationale.md#agent-files-name-no-project)).
377	
378	**How to apply:** state the rule and its mechanism in the agent-file, and leave the evidence trail
379	in the records of the project that earned it (the cycle-record, Todo entries), reachable from the
380	commit that changed the agent-file. Dates are fine, since a date names a moment, not an adopter. A
381	specimen in the scheme's own notation (an example version, an example bookmark name) is a use, not a
382	reference, per the same distinction [Versions live in the version-of-record
383	only](#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only) draws.
384	
385	## Speculation marker
386	
387	Durable text the agent writes (agent-files, `notes/`, commit bodies, the cycle-record) should stick
388	to observations and direct descriptions of the code or data. If a mechanism, hypothesis, or causal
389	claim enters the text, prefix it with "We think ..." (a royal "we") so a reader can tell the
390	measured from the inferred ([why](rationale.md#speculation-marker)).
391	
392	**How to apply:** observations and factual descriptions need no marker. Prefix with "We think ..."
393	(or a close variant like "Our guess is ...") when the claim is a mechanism ("X wins because Y caches
394	better"), a cause ("the drift was due to thermal state"), a prediction ("this should scale
395	linearly"), or any reasoning not directly supported by the data on hand.
396	
397	## Plain synopsis after technical explanations
398	
399	When a conversational reply centers on a technical explanation (measurement theory, statistics,
400	hardware behavior), end it with a short plain-language synopsis, no jargon and no symbols, so the
401	reader can check their understanding against the technical version
402	([why](rationale.md#plain-synopsis-after-technical-explanations)).
403	
404	**How to apply:** conversation only, not notes files (a notes entry should already lead with the
405	why). Mark it clearly (e.g. "The plain version:"). A reply that is already plain needs no synopsis.
406

file.content:
# Prose and durable text

How long-lived text is written on this project: the prose shape, the punctuation rules, and the
commit-title identity. Read this before writing durable text (notes files, commit messages, doc
comments, the cycle-record).

Universal file, shared with the template repository. A proposed change is edited here and converges
at the template ([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)). Project-local
content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).

## Prose form

([why](rationale.md#prose-form))

Long-lived prose on this project follows one basic shape: a short intro that explains the *why* or
the high-level *what*, sharpened to a *problem statement* where a surface calls for one (see
[Problem-first shape](#problem-first-shape)), then a `-` bullet list for the details. The width
numbers and the wrap discipline live in [Line widths](#line-widths) below, their one home. One fact
per bullet or sub-bullet beats a paragraph packing several. Avoid wall-of-prose paragraphs: they
hide the structure that bullets make scannable. Punctuation that joins clauses without naming their
relationship is the same failure at sentence scale. See [Semicolons](#semicolons) and [Typeable
punctuation only](#typeable-punctuation-only).

Surfaces that use this shape:

- Module / function / struct / field doc comments in `.rs` files. See [Doc
  comments](code.md#doc-comments-on-every-file-function-and-method).
- Commit message bodies (both work-repo and agent-repo). The title is the commit-specific add-on.
  See [The per-rung flow](../AGENTS.md#the-per-rung-flow).
- The cycle-record, `TODO.md > ## In Progress`. See [The In Progress
  block](notes.md#the-in-progress-block).
- Todo entries in `TODO.md` when an entry needs more than one line of detail. Pure one-liners are
  still fine.

Bullet *content* differs by surface:

- **Commit bodies**: the [Problem-first shape](#problem-first-shape) for finished work, arranged by
  [Commit-body form](#commit-body-form) below. What is specific to a commit:
  - the problem statement defines any word the title assumes, since the title is what a reader meets
    first and it answers the problem
  - **no file list.** The diff and `git show --stat` are the mechanical record, so restating them is
    a second copy that can drift from the first. An import of a thousand files is one change
  - these are claims a reader has to follow, so they are sentences rather than fragments. A bullet
    wanting a paragraph belongs in the cycle-record instead
  - the **deliberation** stays out: alternatives weighed, evidence, dates, costs accepted. Those
    live in the cycle-record, the `## Todo` entry, and the session the `ochid:` trailer names, each
    reachable from the commit by construction. The problem itself is a *why* and belongs here
- **Cycle-record / todo**: bullets are conceptual (design points, structural notes, the "what landed
  and why" at a notch above file-list granularity). Never a copy of the commit's edit list. The diff
  is the mechanical record, the commit body the problem and solution, the cycle-record the design
  thinking, and none restates another.
- **Doc comments**: bullets are whatever structure fits (fields, cases, invariants).

### Leads are labels, unmarked

In a list item or a numbered step, a lead is a short label ending in a colon, with no markup, and
the sentence after it is complete without it:

```
1. Backfill: fill every as-built ladder whose commits have landed, before anything else.
```

- Label names, sentence instructs: a reader's eye takes bold at the head of an item as the item's
  name and resumes at the plain text expecting a full sentence, so a bold lead that is the
  sentence's own verb or subject (`**Backfill** every as-built ladder ...`) loses its imperative to
  the reader who skips it. Measured 2026-08-21, at the review of the rule that example is from: the
  reviewer read "every as-built ladder" and stopped, with nothing telling them what to do.
- The inverted case: a rule stated in bold is the same failure inverted. When the bold is a whole
  sentence and the plain text is commentary, the reader who skips bold reads the commentary as the
  rule. The fix is the same: a short name as the label, the rule as the plain sentence. The hard
  rules in AGENTS.md are the instance, and the names they gained are greppable and survive a
  renumbering.
- Definitions: the same shape, `Term: what it means.` A period after a bold term (`**Term.** ...`)
  reads as a heading, which is the label reading again.
- No markup on the label: bold is what makes the eye treat the lead as a heading and skip it, and
  the agent-files are read by an agent, which needs no emphasis. The colon alone marks the label
  (wink, 2026-08-21).
- The price: one word of redundancy, paid on purpose: the label is skippable, the sentence is not.

### One spelling per term

A defined term has one spelling, everywhere: `work-repo` and `agent-repo` are always hyphenated,
`agent-files`, `version-of-record`, `dual-repo`, and `as-built` likewise, and no rule varies the
spelling by how the term is used. Terminology in AGENTS.md defines the terms, and this section is
where the spelling rule lives, since a glossary is read for meaning rather than for spelling.

### Bullet form

A bullet is a full sentence, capitalized and ending in a period or question mark, unless the list
is a plain list of things (files, names, options), which takes neither. A list is all one or all
the other. A sentence never opens with a lower-case name (`squash-push`, `rationale.md`), it is
recast so the name is not the first word.

### Line widths

Every width number lives here and nowhere else: the other files and sections link here rather than
restating one, so a change is a single edit and the copies cannot drift. Consolidated 2026-08-09,
when the body width moved and the restatements had to be hunted.

- **Prose**, all durable text: wrap at <=100 cols, bullet continuations indented two spaces.
- **Source**, doc comments and inline comments included: <=100 cols, which is rustfmt's default
  `max_width` (enforcement notes in [code.md](code.md#line-width)).
- **Commit titles**: <=50 chars.
- **Commit bodies**: <=75 cols, the Linux kernel patch standard. It replaced git's older 72
  convention here 2026-08-09, and published bodies keep the wrap they shipped with.

The widths are wrap defaults, not absolutes (the title cap excepted). Existing text re-wraps when
touched, no mass sweeps. Write to the full width: wrap near the limit rather than imitating the
narrow wrap of older text, and a line that reads better long stays long (an URL, a literal report
row, indented code in a comment).

### Problem-first shape

`## In Progress` cycle blocks, `## Todo` entries, and commit bodies use a sharper form of the same
shape: a problem, then how it is answered, then the steps that get there.

- **Problem statement** (the why): one or two sentences. Don't pad with intent, don't restate what
  follows it.
- **Solution statement** (the what/how): what is done about the problem, in broad terms, answering
  whatever question the problem statement raises. Surface-specific rules are in [Bullet content
  differs by surface](#prose-form) above.
- **Plan bullets** (the what/when), the steps. Formality differs by surface:
  - In Progress: a committed ladder, one step per commit. See [Conventional-commit
    shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--commit) for the per-step title + `(current)` /
    `(done)` form.
  - Todo entries: rough informal bullets, no numbering, formalized only when the entry is picked up
    into a cycle.

**Timing decides whether the solution statement is provisional, not whether it is written.** A cycle
writes one at Preparation, before the work, and revises it as steps land. The close-out's commit
body carries the final one. A `## Todo` entry's is provisional in the same way. Only a commit body's
is settled, because a commit is finished by the time it has one. The earlier rule here said a plan
was for work not yet done and a solution for work that is, which left a cycle unable to say at its
opening what it intended to do.

### Commit-body form

The specimen is [commit-model.md](commit-model.md). A commit body is the [Problem-first
shape](#problem-first-shape) with one addition: a body whose
problem has several sub-problems arranges them by a fixed recursion, so a reader knows what any
bullet is from its marker and its depth. The earlier statement, "a problem statement then a solution
statement, both broad", left that arrangement to taste, and taste converged slowly and separately.

- **An intro paragraph states the general problem**, and defines any word the title assumes. It is
  mandatory. [Prose form](#prose-form) wants it regardless, and a body opening on a bullet is a body
  a `--body` flag can mistake for an option. The problem is *this commit's*, never the cycle's: the
  cycle's problem lives in the In Progress block, and a body whose problems outnumber what the diff
  resolves is describing something larger than the commit.
- **`*` bullets are the problem's facets**: sub-problems that decompose the intro's general problem,
  not a grab-bag of unrelated fixes. A body reaching for unrelated problem bullets is usually asking
  to be more than one commit.
- **`-` bullets are solutions**, and every `-` sits under a `*`, solving that facet. A `-` with no
  `*` above it reads as a solution to nothing, so there are no top-level solutions: a solution that
  retires every facet at once is written under each, or the facets are one.
- **One facet is the trivial commit**: the intro, one `*`, one or more `-` under it. Not a second
  form, the general form at its smallest.
- **A bookend body is a pointer**: an opening or closing commit resolves no problem of its own, so
  its body is the intro paragraph alone, naming the cycle by its title and pointing at its record,
  the In Progress block. No `*`, no `-`.

**The markers are typed on purpose**: `*` always means problem, `-` always means solution, and the
pairing is what a reader counts on: the `-` answers the `*` above it, with no rule to consult. The
typing also keeps history greppable (`^\* ` finds every facet, `^ - ` every solution). Bodies are
read as plain text, in `jj log` and in terminals, where the markers survive, and if a renderer ever
flattens them the indentation still carries the structure. So the mixed markers are deliberate, and
a linter's consistent-marker rule is wrong to normalize them.

Unchanged by this: no version in title or body, no file list, no deliberation, titles per
[Conventional-commit shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--commit).

### Semicolons

Prose carries no semicolons. A semicolon appears only in code (code spans, fenced code, source
files), where it is syntax rather than prose. The structure a semicolon would have joined is written
explicitly instead:

- **Two claims** take a period, each half standing as its own sentence ("The diff empties. The
  history keeps the record.").
- **A continuation** takes a comma with a conjunction, when one half carries the other's thought
  onward rather than making its own claim.
- **A list hiding in prose** (`A; B; C` inside a sentence or bullet) breaks into sub-bullets so the
  structure shows. List items that themselves contain commas restructure the same way rather than
  separating with semicolons.

The code allowance is why a bare byte scan cannot enforce the rule: a checker blanks the code first,
then expects zero.

The agent-files (`AGENTS.md`, `custom*`, `agent-data/*`) carry no historical exemption and are swept
to zero. Any other historical file keeps its existing semicolons only until it is touched: a commit
that edits a file makes that whole file's prose semicolons owed, code spans exempt, and the cycle
pays them in a penultimate rung of its own, or in its one commit when single-step, using the joins
above, so the touching rung's diff reads as its change alone. What is owed still follows from
touching the file, and only the payment moves. New prose is written correct and is never a sweep
item. A file whose count means rewriting rather than repunctuating becomes its own cycle. Files
outside a cycle's diff are never converted, since that is a sweep and sweeps are their own cycle.
Source-file comments are prose under this rule (see [code.md](code.md#comments-are-prose)).

### Typeable punctuation only

Durable text uses punctuation that can be typed at a terminal. The prohibition is on *authoring*,
not presence: a file may legitimately hold a banned character it transcribed (see below), so a byte
scan is not the rule and a sweep needs the authored/transcribed judgment. Banned from authoring:
`—`, `–`, `…`, `→`. None can be entered without a compose key or a paste, so none can be grepped
for, and an em dash next to option syntax reads as another flag. Like the semicolon rule above, the
agent-files are swept to zero and any other file converts whole when a cycle touches it, paid in
the same penultimate rung as the semicolons (specimens and transcriptions aside, below). A banned
character costs nothing to write and is paid on every read, so the rule is not softer than that.

`…` becomes `...` and `→` becomes `->`. The dashes have no single replacement, because an em dash
usually stands in for a structural decision that was not made. Make the decision:

- **A bullet's title and its body sharing a line** is a heading and a paragraph. Make the body
  sub-bullets.
- **A term and its definition** (`jj diff`, `<base>`, a flag) takes a colon, which keeps a glossary
  or a command list at one line per entry.
- **A prose aside** takes a comma, parentheses, or two sentences. Often the aside should just go.

Converting a heading moves its anchor. The em dash strips but the spaces on both sides survive, so
`## A — B` slugs to `#a--b` while its colon form slugs to `#a-b` (see [Markdown anchor
links](notes.md#markdown-anchor-links)). Re-point inbound links in the same commit.

Scope is the same as [Speculation marker](#speculation-marker), plus commit titles and everything
under `src/`: doc comments, inline comments, and any user-visible string. Source is the surface a
human edits and greps most, so an untypeable character costs more there than in prose. A code span
is not exempt by itself. Naming the character is a specimen and stays, which is how this section
names them. A banned character doing a job is a use and converts: `` `.expect(…)` `` becomes
`` `.expect(...)` ``.

Text quoted from outside this repo's prose (tool output, an error message, an already-published
commit title) is transcribed, not written, so it keeps its characters, whether or not it sits in a
code span. It matters most for commit titles: converting one stops it matching `git log --grep` and
breaks the verbatim identity that [Conventional-commit
shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--commit) requires between a commit title and its ladder
rung.

### Conventional-commit shape (ladder / commit)

([why](rationale.md#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--commit))

A ladder step and its commit description share a *title* shape, a [Conventional
Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/) title (`<type>: <desc>`, an optional
`(scope)` after the type: `feat(push): ...`) over [Prose form](#prose-form) detail. They differ in
the title's marker (below) and in bullet *content*: commit bodies take the [Commit-body
form](#commit-body-form), the ladder's are conceptual (see "Bullet *content* differs by surface"
above). The shared template:

```
<title>                          # <title> is the commit's `<type>: <desc>`
<optional prose intro>
  - <optional item>
    <optional prose intro>
      - <optional sub-item>
      ...
```

The two surfaces apply it as:

- **Ladder step** (`TODO.md` `## In Progress`): the rung is `- [<title>][M] (marker)`: the title
  reference-linked to the rung's subsection via `[M]: #<slug>` in the file's `# References` (the
  closing rung linked like the rest), and the `(current)` / `(done)` marker. Its position in the
  list is its position in the ladder. The last rung is the close-out and its text says so. Detail
  lives not on the rung but in the block's `Ladder details` subsection headed by the rung's exact
  title (see the protocol's [Opening](../AGENTS.md#opening)), bulleted, never `;`-joined inline.
- **Commit description**: no prefix. The title is the first line, and the body is the prose (see
  [Commit description](../AGENTS.md#commit-description)).

The title is **identical** across both for a given step, so a step's ladder entry and its commit
title line up verbatim. A `Ladder details` subsection heading carries the same title, a third
surface on every rung (the closing rung's exists only when close-out gotchas occurred: see the
protocol's [Opening](../AGENTS.md#opening)). Pick the commit title first and reuse it.

That identity is **per step**, not per cycle: each step in a cycle gets its own distinct descriptive
title, never one shared cycle title uniquified by a step marker. The block's title heading carries
the *cycle title*, the bare name no multi-step commit carries (see the bookends below). To keep a
cycle's commits collectable with one `git log --grep`, give the step titles a common greppable stem
(e.g. `config loader`).

**Cycle bookend titles**: a multi-step cycle's bookend commits are the cycle title plus a suffix, "
opening" and " closing", same type (`feat: dynamic warmup opening` /
`feat: dynamic warmup closing`), so one `git log --grep "<cycle title>"` returns the pair that
brackets the ladder. The bare cycle title is the cycle's *name*: the block's title heading carries
it, and no multi-step commit does, which is also what keeps the closing rung's subsection anchor
clear of the title heading's. A single-step cycle's one commit is the cycle and keeps the bare
title, in both repos and in its one ladder rung ([Cycle shape](../AGENTS.md#cycle-shape)). The type
repeats across the pair even though the bookends are mostly bookkeeping: identical prefixes make
them scannable. Rungs between keep their own titles on the stem.

### Commit titles and descriptions

([why](rationale.md#commit-titles-and-descriptions))

The vocabulary over the structure: [Conventional-commit
shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--commit) holds what a title and body are shaped like, and
this section holds what may fill them. The title is a [Conventional
Commit](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/), `<type>: <short description>` with an optional
`(scope)`, at the width in [Line widths](#line-widths). The body is the [Commit-body
form](#commit-body-form), wrapped per Line widths, with no version in title or body, no file list,
and no deliberation. `vc-x1 push` gives both repos' commits the same title and body. `ochid:` is
the body's last line, stamped by push, and a breaking change uses the hyphenated
`BREAKING-CHANGE:` trailer key.

#### Conventional commit types

The common types: `feat`, `fix`, `refactor`, `test`, `docs`, `chore`. A type beyond the common set
is a declared one ([Project-declared types](#project-declared-types)), and a title check admits
exactly the two vocabularies.

#### Conventional commit scopes

A scope names a component as its user would name it (a subcommand, a repo), never a file or
directory, and is omitted when there is none. A declared type's scope slot carries its
declaration's vocabulary instead ([Project-declared types](#project-declared-types)).

#### Project-declared types

Beyond the common types, a project may declare its own when a recurring kind of work deserves one
searchable token. The declaration names the type, its scope vocabulary, and its description
grammar, so a reader can parse the titles and a title check can admit them by name, and the scope
slot then carries what the declaration says rather than a component. A project's own declarations
live in its `custom.md`, and the set declares for itself:

- `agent-files`, the set's own lifecycle: `agent-files(<scope>): vX.Y.Z`, the description being the
  agent-files version in its `v` spelling ([Agent-files
  version](versioning.md#agent-files-version)), which keeps the formulaic titles unique and is the
  one version a title may carry ([Versions live in the version-of-record
  only](#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only)).
  - The two scopes:
    - `proposal`, outbound work for others to adopt. The cycle bumps the agent-files version, and
      the title names the new one.
    - `adoption`, inbound. The cycle copies the source's version file, and the title names what it
      took.
  - Who proposed to whom, or adopted from whom, is the message record's `from:` and `to:`, never
    the title's.
  - `git log --grep 'agent-files('` finds every agent-files title, the recurring type being the
    token that collects the thread.

### Steps are named, not numbered

A step has a title and no number. Nothing in a ladder rung or a commit gives a step an ordinal: a
rung's place in the list already *is* its place in the ladder, so a number beside it would restate
the position and then have to be maintained.

- **The title is the identifier.** A record points at a step by its title, a plain greppable
  mention, which is why the title is verbatim-identical across the three surfaces.
- **Unambiguous, not globally unique.** Two titles must be distinguishable where a title is
  resolved: within its own cycle's block, so a ladder rung names one step and its subsection heading
  one anchor, since a repeated slug silently dedupes to the first one. Across the repo's history a
  title may repeat.
- **Nothing renumbers.** Inserting, reordering or dropping a step edits the ladder list and nothing
  else. On an unlanded topic bookmark the rungs that already committed an older ladder come along.
  See [Cycles run on a bookmark](../AGENTS.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark).
- **`## Todo` is ordered, not numbered**: priority is file order ([Todo
  format](notes.md#todo-format)), so no rank number exists to be cited (the numbered form retired
  2026-08-27).

### Versions live in the version-of-record only

No version appears in durable prose: not in a ladder rung, a commit title, or a commit body. The
manifest is the version's only written home (see [versioning.md](versioning.md)), and a commit's
version is read from that file at that commit
([why](rationale.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only)). The one exception is the set's
own version in an `agent-files` title, wherever that title appears ([Project-declared
types](#project-declared-types)): it names an agreed text, not a build, and naming which is the
title's job.

**No surface records a version.** Which commit a version names is read from the manifest at that
commit, and "what shipped in 0.42.0" is answered by `git log` on the manifest, not by a list kept in
prose. The earlier chores as-built rungs and `## Done` entries carried versions beside commit SHAs,
and retired with the records they lived in ([Cycle-record](../AGENTS.md#cycle-record)).

## Agent-files name no project

An agent-file states rules and mechanisms. It never names an adopter, an adopter's history, or an
adopter's versions. The vc-x1 *CLI* and its versions are tool facts every adopter shares and stay.
What is barred is an adopter's repo appearing in universal text
([why](rationale.md#agent-files-name-no-project)).

**How to apply:** state the rule and its mechanism in the agent-file, and leave the evidence trail
in the records of the project that earned it (the cycle-record, Todo entries), reachable from the
commit that changed the agent-file. Dates are fine, since a date names a moment, not an adopter. A
specimen in the scheme's own notation (an example version, an example bookmark name) is a use, not a
reference, per the same distinction [Versions live in the version-of-record
only](#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only) draws.

## Speculation marker

Durable text the agent writes (agent-files, `notes/`, commit bodies, the cycle-record) should stick
to observations and direct descriptions of the code or data. If a mechanism, hypothesis, or causal
claim enters the text, prefix it with "We think ..." (a royal "we") so a reader can tell the
measured from the inferred ([why](rationale.md#speculation-marker)).

**How to apply:** observations and factual descriptions need no marker. Prefix with "We think ..."
(or a close variant like "Our guess is ...") when the claim is a mechanism ("X wins because Y caches
better"), a cause ("the drift was due to thermal state"), a prediction ("this should scale
linearly"), or any reasoning not directly supported by the data on hand.

## Plain synopsis after technical explanations

When a conversational reply centers on a technical explanation (measurement theory, statistics,
hardware behavior), end it with a short plain-language synopsis, no jargon and no symbols, so the
reader can check their understanding against the technical version
([why](rationale.md#plain-synopsis-after-technical-explanations)).

**How to apply:** conversation only, not notes files (a notes entry should already lead with the
why). Mark it clearly (e.g. "The plain version:"). A reply that is already plain needs no synopsis.

# vc-x1 config file

Configure the work-repo of a dual repo system. The other repo, we call the agent-repo, is
also a markdown configuration file typically named .vc-config.md.

The code blocks in these config files are in toml format and these blocks are logically
concatenated in the order written here and those become the information used for configuring
the system. The [vc-config.md](vc-config.md) contains the documentation for the
various toml tables used for configuration and it is also used during compilation to define
the valid contents of this file.

The file [vc-config-test.md](vc-config-test.md) is a simple version of this file.
(I think we might rename the file vc-config-test.md to vc-config-model.md and it should
also contain every table and key/value pair showing typical or default values, my thoughts)

The two repos
- work [[1]]
- bot [[2]]
```toml
[repos]
work = "."
agent = ".claude"
```

The agent-file family this repo belongs to: its member name and the sibling repos it answers to
- member [[3]]
- template [[4]]
- messages [[5]]
```toml
[family]
member = "zc-ring-x1"
template = "../vc-x1-template"
messages = "../vc-x1-messages"
```

The validation commands, each element one invocation, run in order by `vc-x1 validate`. The
library is linted alone, `no_std`, then everything with every feature, `std` included
- full [[6]]
- fast [[7]]
```toml
[validate]
full = [
  "cargo fmt",
  "python3 notes/prose-check.py",
  "cargo clippy --lib -- -D warnings",
  "cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings",
  "cargo test --all-features",
  "cargo install --path . --locked",
]
fast = ["python3 notes/prose-check.py", "cargo test --bins"]
```

# References

[1]: vc-config.md#reposwork
[2]: vc-config.md#reposbot

726	The last cycle's finished record, moved here whole by its closing commit and deleted by the next
727	opening ([Cycle-record](AGENTS.md#cycle-record)). Earlier cycles are in the landmark commit's copy
728	of this section, and the cycles before the rule in the frozen [notes/chores/](notes/chores) and
729	[notes/done.md](notes/done.md).
730	
731	### refactor: make mpsc v3 producer and consumer states private
732	
733	#### Problem
734	
735	MPSC v3's `ConsumerState`, every field of it, `MpscConsumer::st`, and `MpscProducer::segs` are
736	`pub(super)`, though the consumer's doc comment calls its state private. Only tests reach them from
737	outside their files: `positions_survive_the_wrap` in `mod.rs` sets the consumer's position and
738	resume positions, and the `free_segments` test helper reads the producer's segments.
739	
740	#### Solution
741	
742	`ConsumerState`, its fields, `MpscConsumer::st`, and `MpscProducer::segs` are private to their
743	files. The test `positions_survive_the_wrap` stays in `mod.rs` and starts its consumer the way
744	production does: it writes the checkpoint the claim reads, through `Segments::store_consumer`, and
745	checks the wrap in the checkpoint the consumer's release writes back, so it touches no consumer
746	field. `free_segments` reads the ring's segments instead of a producer's, so four
747	tests that built their ring inline bind it first. The consumer's doc comment now opens as the
748	producer's do, `struct ConsumerState` is the consumer's state, and names the handle and the guard
749	as intra-doc links.
750	
751	#### Acceptance check
752	
753	`grep -n "pub(super)" src/mpsc/v3/consumer.rs src/mpsc/v3/producer.rs` lists no field and no
754	struct, only functions, `grep -n "\.st\.\|prod\.segs" src/mpsc/v3/mod.rs` finds nothing, and
755	`positions_survive_the_wrap` passes.
756	
757	Passed: the two files keep `pub(super)` on functions alone, `mod.rs` has no `.st.` and no
758	`prod.segs`, and `positions_survive_the_wrap` passes, failing when its checkpoint is not written.
759	
760	#### Ladder
761	
762	- refactor: make mpsc v3 producer and consumer states private (done)
763	
764	#### Deliberation
765	
766	- Keep the state struct: the read guard borrows `&mut ConsumerState`, so its public type stays
767	  `MpscReadSlot<'c, T, W>` without the handle's lifetime and mode.
768	  - Inlining the fields into the handle would make the guard borrow the handle, adding `'a` and `M`
769	    to the guard's type.
770	  - Borrowing the three fields the guard uses one at a time would drop the struct, at a larger
771	    guard, and is left for a later look.
772	- No getters or setters: private fields used directly keep the disjoint field borrows the reserve
773	  loop relies on, and a trivial accessor would guard no invariant.
774	- Seed the wrap test through the checkpoint, not a test-only setter and not a move: the test then
775	  runs the claim's and the release's real resume path and touches no private consumer state.
776	  - Moving it into a test module in `consumer.rs`, the first try, worked but imported `mod.rs`'s
777	    test helpers as `super::super::tests`, made `pub(super)` for it.
778	- MPSC v3 only: spsc v3, spsc v4, and mpsc v2 keep `pub(super)`, since the versions record the
779	  design's evolution and their differences are the point, the user's call.
780	- The producer's `segs` joined the pushed commit, amended and retitled while the bookmark was a

The last cycle's finished record, moved here whole by its closing commit and deleted by the next
opening ([Cycle-record](AGENTS.md#cycle-record)). Earlier cycles are in the landmark commit's copy

### refactor: make mpsc v3 producer and consumer states private

#### Problem

MPSC v3's `ConsumerState`, every field of it, `MpscConsumer::st`, and `MpscProducer::segs` are
`pub(super)`, though the consumer's doc comment calls its state private. Only tests reach them from
outside their files: `positions_survive_the_wrap` in `mod.rs` sets the consumer's position and
resume positions, and the `free_segments` test helper reads the producer's segments.

#### Solution

`ConsumerState`, its fields, `MpscConsumer::st`, and `MpscProducer::segs` are private to their
files. The test `positions_survive_the_wrap` stays in `mod.rs` and starts its consumer the way
production does: it writes the checkpoint the claim reads, through `Segments::store_consumer`, and
checks the wrap in the checkpoint the consumer's release writes back, so it touches no consumer
field. `free_segments` reads the ring's segments instead of a producer's, so four
tests that built their ring inline bind it first. The consumer's doc comment now opens as the
producer's do, `struct ConsumerState` is the consumer's state, and names the handle and the guard
as intra-doc links.

#### Acceptance check

`grep -n "pub(super)" src/mpsc/v3/consumer.rs src/mpsc/v3/producer.rs` lists no field and no
struct, only functions, `grep -n "\.st\.\|prod\.segs" src/mpsc/v3/mod.rs` finds nothing, and
`positions_survive_the_wrap` passes.

Passed: the two files keep `pub(super)` on functions alone, `mod.rs` has no `.st.` and no
`prod.segs`, and `positions_survive_the_wrap` passes, failing when its checkpoint is not written.

#### Ladder

- refactor: make mpsc v3 producer and consumer states private (done)

#### Deliberation

- Keep the state struct: the read guard borrows `&mut ConsumerState`, so its public type stays
  `MpscReadSlot<'c, T, W>` without the handle's lifetime and mode.
  - Inlining the fields into the handle would make the guard borrow the handle, adding `'a` and `M`
    to the guard's type.
  - Borrowing the three fields the guard uses one at a time would drop the struct, at a larger
    guard, and is left for a later look.
- No getters or setters: private fields used directly keep the disjoint field borrows the reserve
  loop relies on, and a trivial accessor would guard no invariant.
- Seed the wrap test through the checkpoint, not a test-only setter and not a move: the test then
  runs the claim's and the release's real resume path and touches no private consumer state.
  - Moving it into a test module in `consumer.rs`, the first try, worked but imported `mod.rs`'s
    test helpers as `super::super::tests`, made `pub(super)` for it.
- MPSC v3 only: spsc v3, spsc v4, and mpsc v2 keep `pub(super)`, since the versions record the
  design's evolution and their differences are the point, the user's call.
- The producer's `segs` joined the pushed commit, amended and retitled while the bookmark was a
  draft, the user's call, rather than a cycle of its own. The tests read the ring's segments, the
  same addresses, so the producer needs no accessor.

  intra-doc links, which `cargo doc --document-private-items` resolves.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""reflow.py rewraps Rust comment blocks to a column width, moving lines and never words.

Usage:

    python3 notes/reflow.py [--width N] FILE [LINE ...]

- With LINE numbers, reflow.py rewraps the comment blocks holding those lines. Without them, it
  rewraps every comment block in FILE.
- A comment block is a run of lines that each start, after indentation, with the same `///`,
  `//!`, or `//`. A comment that follows code on its line, such as an `// OK:` comment, is not a
  block and is left as it is.
- reflow.py keeps a block's structure: paragraphs, `-` and `1.` list items at any depth with their
  continuation lines, `#` headings, blank comment lines, reference definitions, and fenced code,
  which it leaves untouched.
- A word longer than the width stays whole on its own line, since Line widths lets a line that
  reads better long stay long.
- reflow.py checks that each block's words are the same, in the same order, after the rewrap, and
  stops without writing the file when they are not.

The width is prose.md's Line widths for source, 100 by default.
"""

import re
import sys
import textwrap

COMMENT = re.compile(r'^(\s*)(///|//!|//)( |$)')
ITEM = re.compile(r'^( *)(- |\d+\. )')


def prefix_of(line):
    """prefix_of returns a comment line's indentation and marker, or None for any other line."""
    m = COMMENT.match(line)
    return m.group(1) + m.group(2) if m else None


def blocks_of(lines):
    """blocks_of returns the (start, end) line index ranges, inclusive, of every comment block."""
    out, i = [], 0
    while i < len(lines):
        pre = prefix_of(lines[i])
        if pre is None:
            i += 1
            continue
        j = i
        while j + 1 < len(lines) and prefix_of(lines[j + 1]) == pre:
            j += 1
        out.append((i, j))
        i = j + 1
    return out


def reflow_block(block, width):
    """reflow_block returns a comment block's lines rewrapped to `width` columns."""
    pre = prefix_of(block[0])
    texts = [line[len(pre) + 1:] if line[len(pre):].startswith(' ') else '' for line in block]
    # Each unit is ('raw', text) kept as it is, or ('wrap', first indent, next indent, words).
    units, fenced = [], False
    for t in texts:
        if t.lstrip().startswith('```'):
            fenced = not fenced
            units.append(('raw', t))
        elif fenced or t == '' or t.startswith('#') or re.match(r'^\[[^\]]+\]: ', t):
            units.append(('raw', t))
        elif m := ITEM.match(t):
            lead = m.group(1) + m.group(2)
            units.append(['wrap', lead, ' ' * len(lead), t[len(lead):]])
        elif units and units[-1][0] == 'wrap' and t.startswith(units[-1][2]) and (
                t[len(units[-1][2]):][:1] != ' ') and not ITEM.match(t):
            units[-1][3] += ' ' + t.strip()
        else:
            units.append(['wrap', '', '', t])
    out = []
    for u in units:
        if u[0] == 'raw':
            out.append(pre + (' ' + u[1] if u[1] else ''))
            continue
        _, first, rest, words = u
        out += textwrap.wrap(words, width, initial_indent=pre + ' ' + first,
                             subsequent_indent=pre + ' ' + rest, break_long_words=False,
                             break_on_hyphens=False)
    return out


def words(lines):
    """words returns the words of comment lines, markers removed, for the same-words check."""
    return ' '.join(line[len(prefix_of(line)):] for line in lines).split()


def reflow(path, linenos=None, width=100):
    """reflow rewraps the comment blocks of `path` holding `linenos`, or all of them, in place."""
    lines = open(path).read().split('\n')
    ranges = blocks_of(lines)
    if linenos:
        want = {n - 1 for n in linenos}
        ranges = [(a, b) for a, b in ranges if any(a <= n <= b for n in want)]
    for a, b in reversed(ranges):
        new = reflow_block(lines[a:b + 1], width)
        if words(new) != words(lines[a:b + 1]):
            sys.exit(f'{path}:{a + 1}: the rewrap changed the words, nothing written')
        lines[a:b + 1] = new
    open(path, 'w').write('\n'.join(lines))


def main(argv):
    width = 100
    if argv[:1] == ['--width']:
        width, argv = int(argv[1]), argv[2:]
    if not argv:
        sys.exit(__doc__)
    reflow(argv[0], [int(n) for n in argv[1:]] or None, width)


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main(sys.argv[1:])

10:+### feat: mpsc v3 deadline sends
11:+
12:+#### Problem
13:+
14:+An MPSC v3 producer bounds a send on a full ring through closures: `send_with` takes an `on_full`
15:+policy called with an attempt count, `send_with_backoff` adds an `on_lost` hook called after each
16:+lost claim race, and `send_wait` sleeps between the policy's calls. A caller who wants "give up
17:+after this long" writes a closure that reads a clock, and the crate is `no_std`, so it has no clock
18:+to offer.
19:+
20:+#### Solution
21:+
22:+Two sends that take times in microseconds instead of closures, behind a new `std` feature, beside
23:+the closure sends until porting their callers decides whether those go.
24:+
25:+- `send_with_x(give_up_us, fill)`: spin on a full ring until there is room or `give_up_us` has
26:+  passed, then `Full`. `0` is one probe and `u32::MAX` waits forever.
27:+- `send_with_backoff_x(spin_us, wait_us, fill)`: spin for up to `spin_us`, then sleep on the
28:+  producers' futex until `wait_us` has passed in all, sleeping again on what is left after an early
29:+  return, then `Full`. Under `NoWake` the sleep is a spin.
30:+- `Wake::wait` takes its timeout per call, replacing `Futex<TIMEOUT_MS>`.
31:+- The `std` feature is off by default, the clock is read in one function, and validation builds
32:+  the library with the feature and without it.
33:+- The v3 callers move to the `_x` sends. If none still needs a closure, `send_with`,
34:+  `send_with_backoff`, and `send_wait` are deleted and the `_x` sends take the plain names.
35:+
36:+#### Acceptance check
37:+
38:+- A test shows `send_with_x` on a full ring returns `Full` no sooner than its deadline and within a
39:+  bound after it, and succeeds once the consumer frees room.
40:+- A test shows `send_with_backoff_x` under `Futex` sleeping on a full ring, woken when the consumer
41:+  frees room, and returning `Full` at `wait_us` when no room comes.
42:+- `cargo clippy` and `cargo test` pass with `--all-features`, and the library builds with the
43:+  feature off.
44:+
45:+#### Ladder
46:+
47:+- [feat: mpsc v3 deadline sends opening][21] (done)
48:+- [feat: mpsc v3 deadline sends behind std][22]
49:+- [refactor: port mpsc v3 callers to the deadline sends][23]
50:+- [refactor: drop mpsc v3 closure sends][24]
51:+- [feat: mpsc v3 deadline sends closing][25]
52:+
53:+#### Deliberation
54:+
55:+- Times, not closures: a send is bounded by a time in microseconds, the user's proposal of
56:+  2026-09-28.
57:+  - A caller who wants another policy composes it from probes, so the closures' flexibility moves
58:+    to the call site rather than being lost.
59:+  - The spin-then-sleep send is today's `send_wait` reshaped, not today's `send_with_backoff`,
60:+    whose backoff is after a lost claim race, not on a full ring.
61:+- Behind `std` for now, the user's call, until a `no_std` clock is chosen.
62:+  - Off by default, since the crate is `no_std`, and the bins and tools that call the sends turn it
63:+    on.
64:+  - The clock is read in one function, so a `no_std` clock replaces it in one place. We think the
65:+    first is Linux's `clock_gettime` through the `libc` the crate already links for the futex.
66:+- Fresh `_x` names during the cycle, the user's call, so old and new sit side by side and callers
67:+  move one at a time.
68:+- Delete only if the port leaves no holdout: the port is the evidence. The lost-race backoff,
69:+  `on_lost`, is the likely holdout, and is either built in or kept.
70:+- The wake count stays wake-all, the user's call: how many sleeping producers the consumer wakes is
71:+  the consumer's choice, not a send's argument, and the next cycle takes it, the Todo `Wake count
72:+  for sleeping producers`.
73:+- v3 only: v0 through v2 keep their closure sends, as built, and iiac-perf's benches call them.
74:+- No version bump on this cycle's commits, the user's explicit bend of 2026-09-28.
75:+  - It covers: the opening's bump and each rung's, so the version-of-record stays `0.18.5`.
76:+  - It does not cover: the closing, which sets the version, nor the dev name, which the opening
77:+    sets as usual.
78:+  - Why: the size of the bump depends on whether the closure sends are deleted, a break, and that
79:+    is decided mid-cycle.
80:+
81:+#### Ladder details

83:+##### feat: mpsc v3 deadline sends opening
84:+
85:+The cycle's setup commit: create and publish the bookmark, delete `## Closed`'s contents, write this
86:+block, add the wake-count Todo, and rename the package and bins to their `-dev` names, with no

91:+A send bounded by time needs a closure that reads a clock the crate cannot offer. Add the `std`

### docs: mpsc v3 doc pass

#### Problem

The MPSC v3 source, `src/mpsc/v3/mod.rs`, `producer.rs`, and `consumer.rs`, wraps its doc comments
and comments near 70 columns, where the source width is 100, per prose.md's [Line
widths](agent-data/prose.md#line-widths). And the examples on `send`, `send_spin`, and
`send_spin_sleep` run 55 to 60 lines each, mostly the same setup, the message type, the region, the
pool, the ring, and the claims, around a send of about five lines.

#### Solution

Rewrap every comment in the three files to the full width, then lighten the examples.

- The rewrap: `python3 notes/reflow.py <file>` on each file, which keeps paragraphs, bullets at
  any depth, headings, and fenced code, and refuses to write a block whose words changed.
- The examples: each method example's setup goes behind rustdoc's `# ` lines, so a reader sees the
  call and its result and the doctest still runs the whole program.
- One complete, visible walkthrough, pool to release, in one home, README.md, compiled and run as a
  doctest, with the `mpsc::v3` module docs and `user-guide.md` linking to it.

#### Acceptance check

- `python3 notes/reflow.py` on each of the three files leaves it unchanged.
- The rewrap rung's diff changes no word: reflow.py's same-words check passed on every block, and
  the rung holds no edit but reflow.py's and `cargo fmt`'s.
- The rendered examples of `send`, `send_spin`, and `send_spin_sleep` each show 15 lines or fewer.
- `cargo test --doc --all-features` passes, the hidden setup and the README.md walkthrough
  included.

#### Ladder

- [docs: mpsc v3 doc pass opening][1] (current)
- [docs: mpsc v3 doc pass rewrap][2]
- [docs: mpsc v3 doc pass examples][3]
- [docs: mpsc v3 doc pass closing][4]

#### Deliberation

- One cycle, two work rungs, the user's call of 2026-10-02: the rewrap first, reviewed as a rewrap,
  then the examples, reviewed line by line, since the rewrap's review rests on no word changing.
- The rewrap is a deliberate sweep, the user's call of 2026-09-29, where Line widths otherwise
  rewraps text only when it is touched.
  - Text only: the words stay, the lines move, with any wording fix left to its own commit.
  - Lines that read better long stay long, as Line widths allows: the `// OK:` comments on `unwrap`
    calls, a URL.

# Commit model

Two commit bodies from the `config loader` cycle in [cycle-model.md](cycle-model.md), shown as
specimens rather than a skeleton: a work rung's body and a bookend's. Copy the shape, not the
words. The rules are in [Commit-body form](prose.md#commit-body-form).

## A work rung

Title: `refactor: split loader from parser`

```
Config loading and parsing are one function, so the CLI cannot load a
config without parsing it and a test cannot parse one without a file on
disk. The move into its own module is what forces the split.

* The two jobs share one function and one error type.
  - `config::loader` finds and reads the file and returns the text with
    its path, so a caller that only wants to know which file was read
    stops there.
  - `config::parser` takes text and returns the schema, so a test hands
    it a string and never touches the filesystem.
* `main` still reaches into the parse result by field.
